content: In physics, a scalar is a fundamental physical quantity that remains unchanged under transformations of the coordinate system. In Newtonian mechanics, this means it is unaffected by rotations or translations of the coordinate system. In the context of relativity, scalars are invariant under Lorentz transformations and space-time translations. Scalars are distinct from vectors, which have both magnitude and direction. For example, the distance between two points in space is a scalar quantity. Other examples include the mass, electric charge, and kinetic energy of an object, as well as the temperature and electric potential at a specific point within a medium. In contrast, the electric field at a point is not a scalar because it requires three numerical components, which depend on the chosen coordinate system, to fully describe it. Similarly, the gravitational force acting on a particle is not a scalar, but its magnitude is. Examples of scalar quantities in Newtonian mechanics include: Electric charge and charge density Mass and mass density Speed (but not velocity or momentum) Temperature Energy and energy density Time Pressure Entropy Negentropy A physical quantity is expressed as the product of a numerical value and a physical unit, rather than just a number. While the numerical value depends on the unit of measurement (e.g., 1 km is equivalent to 1000 m), the scalar quantity itself does not depend on the unit distance or the length of the base vectors in the coordinate system. For instance, the physical distance between two points is independent of the coordinate system's base vector lengths, although the formula used to compute it may vary depending on the coordinate system (e.g., the Euclidean distance formula assumes an orthonormal basis). This property applies to other physical quantities that are not dimensionless as well. In the theory of relativity, coordinate transformations involve exchanges between space and time dimensions. As a result, some quantities that are scalars in classical (non-relativistic) physics must be combined with other quantities and treated as four-dimensional vectors or tensors. For example, charge density, which is a scalar in classical physics, must be combined with the local current density (a three-dimensional vector) to form a relativistic four-vector. Similarly, energy density must be combined with momentum density and pressure to form the stress-energy tensor. A related concept is the pseudoscalar, which remains invariant under proper rotations but changes sign under improper rotations (e.g., reflections). An example of a pseudoscalar is the scalar triple product, which is associated with the signed volume of a parallelepiped. Another example is magnetic charge, as it is mathematically defined, regardless of whether it exists physically.
